utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: One matter regarding the report of Dr. Nedopil. Have you had an opportunity to review the English translation of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I have reviewed and compared the translation, the English translation with the German, and I found the text to be identical, and therefore we accept that it be tendered as evidence and admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you will mark that as the next exhibit. Do you have an extra copy for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We will provide copies to the court before the close of today, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You may retain your copy. Mr. Keegan, if you would provide four copies, one for the record and one for each of the Judges, fine. You may bring in your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. Before starting with the questioning of the expert witness, we would like to tender to the court another written document which has to do to the current regulations of Republika Srpska, dealing with amnesty in accordance with the law on amnesty, which can show how these problems were dealt with in the territory that now belongs to the Republika Srkpsa according to the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Does that law relate to war crimes or does it just relate to what would be considered ordinary crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, it does apply to war crimes as well and mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked at D120 and the report D119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any objection, Mr. Niemann, to 119 and 120?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is no objection to the document at all. I am not sure we necessarily agree with the characterisation of the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. They will be admitted. Are we ready now for Professor Aleksic? Very good. You may bring in Professor Aleksic. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation): I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath, the solemn declaration that has been handed to you? Professor Aleksic (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Vujin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor Aleksic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is your name Dr. Zivojin Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have to rise? Yes, my name is Zivojin Aleksic. I am a Professor and I acquired the doctorate later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Professor, you teach at the Belgrade Law School of Belgrade University?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: To introduce you to the court, will you please tell me how many books and text books you have written and issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a number. I published 26 books. Quite a number of them have been translated into German, English, Russian, French.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me of which institutions you were a member, where you worked, but very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took a master's degree in Lausanne, my doctorate in Belgrade. I completed three levels of the faculty of comparative law, the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, in Luxembourg. I worked in the United Nations in the area of technical assistance. I trained people. I was a member of the World Peace Through Law Movement and I was co-chairman of the World Association of Law Professors, together with Professor Joe Hazzard, that I'm sure the Trial Chamber is familiar with, from Colombia University. We were co-chairmen, the two of us. I don't think there's any need to go into details. In the country I was President of a large number of associations. You see, I'm well advanced in age, so that it's no wonder that I have such experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I think that will be enough. Can you tell us whether you were engaged in certain specific criminal cases and what is your speciality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My speciality is judicial proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Were you engaged in that area to deal with certain world renowned cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever our State was implicated, I participated in trials of the aggressors on the mission in Bonn, those who attacked the military mission in Berlin, the assassins of our ambassador in Stockholm. I trained many experts in Africa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there are many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that will be enough for the Trial Chamber to get an idea about you as an expert. Could you please say something about the position of criminal law of Yugoslavia, its roots, its level of development and also a few words about the system of criminal sanctions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Criminal law follows life, and if we look back into history, distant history, I think it is better for me to speak slowly, because of the interpretation -- in distant history, in the 14th century already we had an extraordinary criminal code, the Dusan Code. Then things changed when in 1918 the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was formed, each of those nations passed its own laws. Later this was shaped into the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, and I must say that we made a compilation of the Austrian law, the German law and partially the French law, so that the provisions are in accordance with European continental law, but we had an ugly period after the end of the Second World War, from 1945 until 1950, when we were under the influence of the Soviet Union in those days, and we then adopted certain rules in the Criminal Code and in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Which were far from anything we could take pride in, so that they disappeared very soon, which means that we departed from the countries of the Eastern bloc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fortunately, as you know, Yugoslavia managed to withdraw from that bloc and we developed a model of the Criminal Code which was changed in time, but what was specific was that each republic and province had its own Criminal Code, and the procedure was common to them. Unfortunately our Yugoslavia disintegrated and Serbia and Montenegro amended those laws to a certain extent, and our law will be further amended now in the aim to develop a central law and code and procedure for the whole of Yugoslavia. At the moment we have a Serbian and a Montenegran law, but there is not much difference between them, and there is also a Criminal Code of Yugoslavia as the more general, and these two as the specific which eliminate the criminal offences which are covered by the former. At least we expect this to become a unified criminal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the system of criminal sanctions? What is the maximum penalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the first penalty we have caution, then fines and then imprisonment. Imprisonment goes up to fifteen years. That is the limit. However, because until recently we had the death penalty in Yugoslavia, we have given the possibility to the court in certain individual cases to decide to substitute the death sentence with 20 years imprisonment. So if I tell your Honours that we have 15 years as a limit and 20 years, I must tell you that 20 years is very exceptional, because it shows that between 15 and 20 there are no intermediate penalties. There is no penalty of 16 or 17 years. There's 15 as a limit and 20 only as a substitute for the death penalty. By constitution the death penalty has been abolished, and we are still discussing the substitute, but 20 years does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Therefore, according to the Federal Criminal Code, there is no death penalty, but a penalty of 20 years is envisaged, which may exceptionally be prescribed from the worst criminal offences -- for the worst forms of the worst criminal offences it is envisaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but the fact that the court, if I may use the term, in normal proceedings that the court will normally pass a sentence up to 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Which are the circumstances envisaged by the law and which the court takes into consideration when deciding which criminal sanction it will pronounce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have an institution called "social danger" and every court -- I don't think that is any novelty -- on the basis of premeditation and criminal intent, but what I would like to tell the Trial Chamber, we do not have premeditation in our criminal code. We have intent and negligence. Intent, we make a distinction between direct criminal intent and possible criminal intent, which is reached when the negligence is so gross that it develops into intent. For instance, you are driving a car with bad brakes believing that nothing will happen. That is possible intent. In negligence we have violent negligence, conscious and unconscious, unconscious negligence being the mildest form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Which are the objectives of criminal sanctions according to our law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Article 1, as in all other laws, it says that the purpose is to prevent the accused from committing further criminal offences. That is number 1. The second is the humane intention, that the person who is prevented from further criminal offences is sought to be reintegrated -- rehabilitated. Then the second part of Article 1 deals with general potential, prevention in the sense of strengthening morality and preventing impermissible actions, and also certain kinds of threats. It is a kind of caution to all others who might consider committing a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us a little more about the individualisation of penalties? To what extent does the court have the possibility to bear in mind all the circumstances of the event and the character of the accused in order to weigh out the sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The individualisation of sanctions -- I'm already an elderly professor, so I look back into history -- is the central effort of every court. I'm sure the court is well aware of this. The greatest problem is the problem of measure, of degree, as anything else in life, how to find the proper measure for a particular person. Our law has given a list of obligatory things that the court must bear in mind, but it is left to the court to assess other circumstances as well that may arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, there is the life before, whether he has a criminal record, how he lived, then motive, then circumstances, then rage and so on, and then in the end there is something that is important, and that is the behaviour of the perpetrator after the commission of the offence. This is something that carries a lot of weight in Yugoslavia, because this behaviour after the offence is indicative of a kind of rehabilitation of the individual and his becoming a useful member of the community.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: To come back to the first element that you mentioned, prior life, as our law puts it, is family life assessed, the character of the accused, the circumstances under which he was brought up, the circumstances in which he was living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these things are assessed, as well as his material position, simply how he stands, what the conditions of life were in which he was brought up. For that purpose one usually calls up the immediate family and relatives, how he behaved at school, in the army and in any other collective environment, in a community, and then we add what I said just now, his behaviour following the commission of the offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: What I would be further interested in is the sentencing and the sanctioning of accomplices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, you are really rejuvenating me, because I have mostly been in the role of me putting the questions, but now it is my former student who is asking me questions, and this is a great pleasure for me. You see, there is a basic rule and that is that each individual is responsible within the framework of his intent. This is something that we took over from the German and Austrian law. The "Code Penale" is not so definite in that respect. Of course, any deviation from within those boundaries it is up to the court to assess, so if we have accomplices, each one of them is responsible within the limits of his intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Could you illustrate this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If somebody agrees with somebody else to break into a shop and to rob it, then three of them do this, their intent was to enter and to appropriate money or goods, but one of them comes across the guard and kills him, so that he would discover them. Then he is responsible for his intent and these other two cannot be responsible for the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: In that case these other two would not be responsible for murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is the case in our law.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We have this institute of a criminal offence, an on-going criminal offence. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Life shows that people who engage in crime do not usually limit themselves to one offence, but sometimes do a series of such offences or simultaneously commit several offences, and in the case of the accomplice -- is that what you were asking me -- again you go within the boundaries of the intent, but the sanctioning, the method we applied was aspiration, no cumulation, aspiration. Aspiration means that the court rules as follows. For each offence committed, he is -- a sentence is pronounced, but the court must bear in mind, and there are six offences three years each, then the sum -- it may not be a sum -- the final sentence may not be the sum, because that would be cumulation, and there is another rule, that it cannot exceed the envisaged maximum. It cannot be more than 15 years. In this case, if you have six criminal offences three years each, that would be 18. It couldn't exceed 15, because 15 is the limit. Secondly, it cannot be a simple sum, because that would be the method of cumulation. I'm sorry if I have to say this, but I'm sure our distinguished court knows this. This method of cumulation has been abandoned in theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask one question on what I think is a matter of interpretation? I think the witness spoke about aspiration as being something distinct from cumulation. "Aspiration" in English doesn't mean that at all. Could you perhaps ask the witness what he has in mind by "aspiration", what was translated as "aspiration"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In Latin -- "aspiration" is from Latin. There are six times three years, for instance, for criminal offences. Cumulation would mean 18 years. Aspiration means taking away a little bit of each and not making a simple sum of those penalties. I don't know if I have explained myself. I hope we understand one another. Yes, in English it doesn't mean anything, but we have taken it over from Latin, and I studied Latin a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: In English it means "hoping".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is aspiration, but the aspiration, "asperatio". Sorry for me -- I am professor. It is usual I give lectures but you are absolutely right. Not aspiration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Aspe ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only aspiration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is similar to sentences being not cumulative but concurrent, concurrent, running with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. Cumulation would in this case be 18 years, but it violates two principles of the aspiration, and that is it cannot exceed the maximum limit envisaged by the law, which is 15 years, and secondly, which is even more important, it cannot be a simple sum of all the penalties, because then it is cumulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Why is that so? Why can it not be -- some systems do have both concurrent and cumulative available to the sentencing Judge so that, for example, if an individual commits two distinct offences, you look at each offence, you determine what is the appropriate sentence, and assuming that the offences are distinct and separate, some systems do allow them to be served cumulatively, meaning you would sentence for offence A, recognising that it had been done, and you would sentence for offence B, recognising that it had been done, and in order to give effect to that, you would then have to combine those two. Why is that not so in your system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for the attention you are showing for what I am saying. I thank the whole Trial Chamber, of course. But this aspiration or concurrence occurs when the offences were committed without a wide time limit in between, for instance in a single day, not at various periods of time. If they occur at various times, then it is possible, but, secondly, in Europe, since the French Revolution certain ideas came to the fore speaking about certain -- giving certain alleviation to or the beneficial treatment of the accused, and this is one of the things whereby the position of the accused is sought to be alleviated, confronted with the machinery of justice: nebis in idem re sum dicta (sic). Various facilities for the accused, which at first glance may not be logical but have a certain indication of our belief in man, in his ability to correct his behaviour and become a useful member of society. It is terrible when justice squeezes out the man. Such a man can never be rehabilitated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: If I may be allowed, your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: There are different theories, are there not, in terms of sentencing? Some people believe there is a role for rehabilitation, other people for punishment, other people for deterrence. There are a number of factors that play into this picture, of course, and I think you spoke of deterrence. You didn't use the word, but I understand what you meant. I guess it would depend on which you considered to be the most important of these various factors or motives or reasons for sentencing, but after the French Revolution you are saying that what became in vogue was rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we can agree on that. Absolutely. Your Honour, I fully agree. Rehabilitation is something that all modern courts of law aspire for. However, it was difficult for this idea to struggle in through history, because an eye for eye and tooth for tooth is still present in the way of thinking of the man in the street in my country, for example, and you know best as a judge how many times you have heard or still hear objections to your concept of justice and imposing sentences. Deterrence is certainly one thing, but I just thought of examples from Medieval times when, for example, people would steal during a public hanging, because people would be watching the hanging transfixed and they wouldn't pay attention to somebody pilfering their wallets. So we have to believe in something. In Yugoslavia I always tell my students that each verdict affects at least seven people, and it can change a person's life definitely, but let us see to what extent, but frankly speaking, sometimes a sentence can destroy a person and his family. I believe that the esteemed chamber shared this opinion and I apologise for saying things that are certainly your views too; no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I, for one, would want to know the seven people who the sentence affects or are we getting too far ....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What seven? First of all, the family, that is to say the spouse, the wife or two or three children, or one child -- I don't know. Then his parents, you know. Then the wife and her parents and that's about seven, and then if there are any siblings, a brother, a sister, etc. I'm sure that you accept that. A person who was sentenced once has a very tough time afterwards trying to find his place under the sun. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have one last question I think on aspiration. It sounds to me as if it is different from the notion of concurrent sentences. Let us take an example of two offences, each being punished with three year's imprisonment. If they were concurrent, the accused would serve only three years. With aspiration, you might add -- you might add pieces of each of them and it might be a total of, say, four years. Is that the way in which your system works?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are putting a question to me as if you were a colleague of my judge colleagues in Yugoslavia. That is what they usually ask and that is how they usually work. However, concurrence does not have to mean the same day. You have pickpockets, for example, who do that as a regular thing. Then the social danger is great because he shows his intent every day and then again they cannot go beyond these two things, the maximum envisaged for that kind of crime and mathematical summing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: But with your permission, your Honour, I understood Judge Stephen's question but I don't know how come we have three years. If we have two sentences of three years each concurrently for two crimes, are there systems in which the accused will spend only three years in prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Then our system is truly different. As the Professor said, he will not be prison for three years but four or more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He have would have to get a larger sentence because otherwise he would be privileged, but not six years, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That explains it precisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Professor, the institute of mitigating the sentence has been prescribed by our law. Can you tell me something about that institute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That institute is quite clear, at least in my opinion. We have the offender. We have the punishment envisaged for that crime. There is always a range involved from one to five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: A minimum and a maximum prescribed by law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I must tell the Chamber, with their permission, that unfortunately most of our analyses -- it is not always a good thing -- show that most of our punishment sentences in Yugoslavia are near the minimum. This may be a surprise, but usually it's the minimum. If it's from 3-7 years, then it's usually 3-4 years that is served. However, mitigation of the sentence. We have the person involved. We have his crime and we have the punishment that is envisaged. His previous life, subjective and objective circumstances, are quite telling, and this can lead to a milder, less strict sentence, but it can also to a more strict sentence. For example, if he abuses a person who he is supposed to take care of, for example if he is a teacher or if he is a guardian and if he is in charge of a certain person, and if he abuses that, that is an aggravating circumstance, or, for example, when we had an epidemic of Smallpox in Belgrade, then very strict sentences were imposed on people who smuggled medicine related to that disease. That is an aggravating circumstance. A mitigating circumstance is, for example, if somebody hits a person with his car but he puts that person in the same car immediately, takes him to the hospital, donates blood for this person, etc., or the previous forms that were filled out in our country also included questions asking whether this person had been decorated or received certain awards, etc., so this was taken into account. If I'm not mistaken, you are looking at the papers that were submitted to the Prosecutor made by Dr. Vasiljavic and Dr. Jankovic. First of all, I must say I am very sorry that Dr. Vasiljavic died but the paper you have is dated, I'm afraid, Mr. Prosecutor, because the data contained there refer to 1982-1988. So they are ten years old. Secondly, that was the period of the SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, when there were five different laws, and a classical, so to speak, situation, of crime, when crimes such as genocide, etc., practically didn't even exist, crimes against humanity. In 1991, when Yugoslavia started falling apart the situation changed. For example, in Belgrade we have a lot of murders. During one year, if you take into account the number of criminal murders, it exceeds that which was relevant for four year periods before that. So my colleagues whom I know and respect made this paper and I wish to draw nevertheless the attention of this court to the fact that the paper is dated. If necessary, I can submit to you a written document on the current situation in criminal law and the criminal judiciary in Montenegro and Serbia now. The closeness of the war brought forth what is called "the Vietnam syndrome" and I believe that a great effort will have to be made both by Yugoslavia and the international community for Yugoslavia to become once again what it was before, a tourist country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is that one of the reasons why our courts now impose sentences which are close to the legal minimum, so if the range envisaged is 5-20 years, if all circumstances are taken into account, nevertheless the sentence is usually 5 years or something similar to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are different theories on that is correct which is absolutely correct. It is always the lower minimum in Yugoslavia that is applied in the case of these sentences. When I talk to our judges they usually find various mitigating circumstances which say that this person is not incorrigible, that he is not ruthless, but I cannot say what the exact reason is. After all, that's the job of the court. Therefore certain things in life that we simply don't know about. For example, there is a standard rule in all countries that out of the total number of children born in any country 100 men are born and 100 women, but then sometimes the advantage of males and females is reversed, but at birth it is 105: 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I wish to ask you something which may only seem outside of your domain, but it is relevant to all of us here, I think. As your job did you study local self-government in our country perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I worked on programmes of study against crime, either general or particular ones, we devoted a great deal of attention to the family as the nuclear cell and all these smaller organisations too. Unfortunately the struggle against crime requires a lot of money, and that's a basic problem in Yugoslavia. I don't know how we're going to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: When you speak of these smaller communities, are you referring to municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. The municipality is the closest to the family. It takes care of the school, of the Red Cross. It solves housing problems, public utilities. It is practically the heartbeat of a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is there an authority which is not entitled to pass decisions but which does exist from an organisational point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the constitution the municipality is the lowest organ. However, because of the fact that our country is so widespread, these municipalities cannot always take care of their entire territory. So, for example, a health centre, municipal health centre can work in different places in different ways in order to help the entire population. So you have these local conferences, etc., etc., but the statute of the municipality has to say where there is going to be a local community, and since this local community is not a constitutional category, it does not have any major functions. This is just a centre that handles matters related to schools, etc. If I remember correctly, they have an assembly of the community, a council of the community and an interesting organ -- I don't know what kinds of results it yields -- and that is the consumers' council. So that is it more or less. Sometimes there are certain ad hoc matters, protection from fires, for instance, then; defence from hail and thunder, more or less this is a centre which is in contact with the municipality and does not pass decisions through its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So it is through the decision of the municipality that the local community is formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And you said there is a council as an executive organ and this consumers' council that takes care of supply, markets, etc.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that it functions rather poorly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I'm interested in this relationship between the assembly and this executive organ of the local community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As elsewhere, the assembly doesn't meet very frequently and the council works all the time practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: But the council works according to the decision of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And the assembly is accountable to the municipality whereas the council is accountable to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is one place within this local self-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The secretary of the local community, is that an organ or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I think this is a paid official who is there to act according to the instructions received from these other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is this an administrative work? Is that what you can say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It has no other authority of the even the council of the local community. The question is whether they have any special authority or is this authority delegated by the assembly. To take an insignificant matter, enrolling into school, then the council informed the assembly how many children of school age there are now on the territory of the local community, and then the municipality decides whether it is sufficient to have, say, one teacher, or whether they need another teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So the local community cannot decide that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is the municipality. The municipality's extended arm, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: To whom is the secretary of the local community responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the President of the council and the President of the council is responsible to the assembly and the President of the assembly of the local community responsible to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And the municipality is the only one that is in charge of reaching these decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Otherwise there would be utter confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have completed my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujin. Cross-examination, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor Aleksic, when was the death penalty abolished, what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The death penalty was abolished when the new constitution of Yugoslavia was adopted of the present day Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was about two years ago, approximately two years ago, I think, and now we have a strange paradox in our criminal law, and you being an excellent lawyer will fully appreciate that. We have a constitution which abolished the death penalty and then there is Serbia that has the death penalty and Montenegro that does not have the death penalty. At any rate I can tell you what the epilogue is. There are no death penalties. There are some that have been pronounced and these poor people are awaiting execution. However, I firmly believe that this will not take place because, after all, the supreme act is the constitution and all these other laws are below that, and I believe that this new criminal law that is being prepared now will resolve the issue and this is paradoxical and you have observed that quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to the abolition by the new constitution and going back to, say, 1992, in what of the republics of the then breaking-up Yugoslavia, if I might call it that, had the death penalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Practically in all republics before 1992 while the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia existed -- that is the paper you have from my colleagues Vasiljavic and Jankovic -- it is said in all these five or eight laws that existed, the death penalty was instituted in all of them. I must tell you that Slovenia held the record in all of that, in some 30 or 40 years not a single penalty had been imposed. When they had a mass killer who had murdered seven or eight women they were fortunate enough that he was considered to be mentally incompetent. So that is why he was not executed either. That was the pre-war situation. In Serbia and Montenegro today you have the situation I already referred to. At present we have four or five death sentences that were imposed and these poor people are waiting to see what will happen, but they hope the constitution will prevail. I personally think, as a law, and I believe that all present here share that view, that there is nothing more terrible than awaiting the execution of a death sentence and unfortunately in all countries this is a penalty that is awaited for years. It's the worst penalty of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just mainly interested in the history of the death penalty. Now, as I understand it, and correct me if I'm wrong, the maximum penalty would be 15 years, because that was a period of time that was considered best to facilitate rehabilitation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that 15 years is certainly one thing. However, all criminological and penological research has shown that any term of imprisonment longer than ten years impairs a person mentally and makes him psychologically mentally handicapped in terms of his further life, but 15 years was the maximum. I imagine that you are aware of the fact that after having served two-thirds of the term due to good behaviour there could be probation or a pardon. So mostly up to 11 years for the gravest delinquents. In practice, however, according to the law, 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not really asking you for your opinion on what you consider to be the best period of time in order to facilitate rehabilitation. I'm really asking you: was the law designed this way because that was considered to be the maximum time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know full well that life and law do not always go hand in hand. According to the law it is 15 years, but during these 40 years I have not encountered a single person in Yugoslavia who served all those 15 years. Usually a person would be released after these 11 years or so. However, sometimes it would happen --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can just interrupt you, Professor. Perhaps you don't know the answer, and if that's right, I will move on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I am asking you what is the law --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Sorry, but I don't think that this kind of reaction is proper. You have received an answer. The Professor said five times now that 15 years is the maximum sentence according to law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the problem is. I truly wish I could help you rather than enter into a polemic with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let's see if we can help. There are three people all at once. I guess the question is; was the law designed to establish a maximum?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the law designed, when it enacted a 15 year maximum, to -- that period was selected because it was considered to be the maximum period of imprisonment that could be endured if rehabilitation was to be effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the law says 15 years. That is what I said at the very outset. Whether 15 years facilitates rehabilitation, I'm sceptical. That's my personal opinion, but 15 years is what the law says, but I did not meet a single prisoner who spent 15 years in jail. Then there is 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking your opinion of what you consider being the maximum period, Professor. You have come here as an expert on the law and I am asking if you understand the basis of the law on the selection of the period 15 years. Now Professor, and I am not in any way attempting to be rude, but if you do not know that and it is perfectly conceivable you don't, then I'll move on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth towards the end of my legal career it would be hard to say I couldn't understand such a question. The law says 15 years. That's the fact of the case. I thought it might be clear both to you and to the Trial Chamber when I say what I say. I understood my coming here not just to be an interpreter of the law but to convey to you the spirit of the law of my land. If you don't want that, then let me say there is 15 years and there's 20 years as a substitute for the death penalty. Now why 15 years was chosen? Because of the gravity of the offence, but the entire system of re-education and penology is designed to encourage persons to improve. It would be a terrible feeling if somebody goes to prison and is discouraged from improving. His reward is the gradual reduction of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have not asked you that particular part, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I just ask you one question. What is the relationship, if you know, between the maximum of 15 years and the goal of rehabilitation? What is the relationship, if there is any, between the establishment of a 15 year maximum and the goal of rehabilitation? There may not be a relationship. It may be this 15 years was established because that would be the time thought that should be given for those offences that were very grave but not so grave that they deserved the death penalty, but if there is a relationship between that maximum and the goal of rehabilitation, I think that's what Mr. Niemann is asking you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The degree of criminal responsibility and the circumstances of the criminal offence enable the court to pronounce the maximum sentence of 15 years. Whether for that individual 15 years is a period during which he can be re-educated I don't know, but I do know that it is a penalty isolating that person because of the gravity of his criminal offence. Somebody can be re-educated in a year or two and can realise that he did something wrong, and this can be just a nightmare from his past, whereas someone else can never recover. They suffer always.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that somebody who would have received the death penalty in Yugoslavia, let us say up to the period of 1992, those persons would not have been considered suitable for rehabilitation and the seriousness of the crime would have been such that it would have dictated that consequence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that you are not inclined to hear my opinions, but I still have to say that I personally do not believe that there is such a person that cannot be -- that condition improve except for mentally retarded people. As for the death penalty it is a very sad phenomenon and the whole of society is against this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not asking you that question. Do you want me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Vujin, I suppose the objection is that the answer is not responsive to the question. Can you answer the question or do you recall the question, Professor? Do you know whether or not when the death penalty was utilised, going back to the period 1992, was it a determination made by the legislator or whatever body passed the law, that that penalty was to be imposed because it was the gravest of offences and it was assumed that persons who commit those offences that are so grave are not capable of being rehabilitated? Rightly or wrongly, was that their feeling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is quite clear that the imposing of a death sentence refers to a person that has to be isolated from society, but not to enter into my opinion, as that doesn't interest you, the death sentence is the total and incorrigible exclusion of man from the society which he is living in, but I have my opinion about that, which I won't convey.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I have an objection, your Honour. We are continuing the discussion on the death penalty, and I think that we shouldn't engage in polemics on the death penalty. I do not see where this is leading us to. We in Yugoslavia have been talking about the death penalty for five years and eventually the Federal constitution abolished the death penalty. I do not see what the intention of the Prosecutor is to have this debate on the death penalty, which is not even envisaged by the rules of procedure of the Tribunal. I think it out of place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence so far from the Professor has concentrated on the issue of rehabilitation, and so far there has been very little attention paid to any of the other objectives of the sanction that is attached to a penalty. I'm endeavouring to explore this. He himself has told us that the death penalty operated up to 1992 and certainly up until very recently in Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I'm merely trying to explore the basis of the philosophy of the penalties and how they operate in Yugoslavia. I think it's a perfectly reasonable line of questioning, having regard to the fact that the Defence has been left at liberty to fully explore the issue of a penalty and the penalty most appropriate for rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I'll overrule your objection, Mr. Vujin. Proceed along. Get us eventually to the point now that the death penalty has been abolished. That's something I am interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will endeavour to get there, your Honour. So there was up until quite recently a measure of penalty, i.e. the death penalty, that operated in cases where rehabilitation was not considered to be appropriate for the particular offender that was being dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that, yes. That is common knowledge. But as an opponent of the death penalty I cannot lay still when we are talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sure, Professor, that you will have plenty of opportunities to express your views on that in other forums, but in this forum we are primarily interested in the -- well, I am principally interested in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For as long as I remain in good health.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, you then said that a 20 year maximum period of imprisonment was introduced and that was for some crimes, and that was in circumstances where the 15 year maximum was not considered appropriate, and in circumstances which followed the abolition of the death penalty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall avoid any personal opinions. The legislator envisaged the death sentence, but he left it to the judge to assess. In the event that the whole case points to the adequacy of the death penalty, the legislator has left it to the judge to turn this into a prison sentence. So this is indicative of a change in the orientation of society. The 20 year sentence is an exceptional measure and a substitute for the death penalty. In this way the legislator has shown his attitude towards a measure that cannot be rescinded, that is final.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now I think that you indicated -- well, the gist that I got from your evidence was that the 20 year maximum that has now been introduced was in a sense an interim measure and the matter was still under discussion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not under discussion. On the contrary, it was the harbinger of the future abolition of the death sentence, because a death sentence cannot be pronounced on a person under 21 years of age and as a substitute in some cases there is the prison term of 20 years. So this was a harbinger of the future abolition of the death sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So under Yugoslav policy there is still provision for the offenders to be dealt with where the sentencing disposition of the court is that the punishment should be the primary focus of the sentence rather than rehabilitation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When a death penalty is imposed according to Yugoslav law, the court says: "I sentence you to death by firing squad but because of such and such circumstances that sentence is being amended to 20 years in prison".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That wasn't quite a question, Professor. Would you like me to repeat it again for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please. I find it very strange that we don't seem to be able to understand one another very well today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I regret that, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me, too. Me, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My question was: the policy is so there is still provision for offenders to be dealt with -- excuse me. I'm trying to -- I will read back my question so I get it precisely. I am not going to be permitted to do so, so I will have to try to remember it. Professor, what I'm saying is that so there's still provision in Yugoslavia -- in the law of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at least where a court, when it's designing the sentencing disposition for a particular offender places a higher emphasis on the fact that the penalty that should be meted out to a particular individual transcends or is more important than the rehabilitation issues that may otherwise be afforded a particular offender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In your question there is something that is not quite clear. As the constitution prohibits the death penalty, we have really a moratorium, because the death penalty is an exceptional measure. It was envisaged early on by law. Now it does not exist. It is not handed down. The explanation given by the court, if you are interested in that, I could study the verdicts of courts, but the fact remains that between 15 and 20 years there are no penalties in between 15 and 20. 20 is only the substitute for the death penalty, and that is what the law says. Now what the court has in mind, what kind of a disposition it has, I can't say. Probably they feel that the death penalty should be used for persons who are harmful to society, but they are substituting that with a 20 year sentence because, after all, all the circumstances are not present for total elimination of the offender.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I must object again. I think there is a misunderstanding, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation, because the translator -- they can only translate one. I couldn't listen to you because I don't speak Serbo-Croat. Mr. Vujin, the witness answered. You have an objection? On what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I apologise. I have an objection, because I think that Mr. Niemann and Mr. Aleksic do not understand one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That's not really the basis for an objection. Let us see if we can end it real quick. They seem to be understanding one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: If I understood the question well, then I would ask that it be repeated to the Professor, so ask him what is the system of sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, I will overrule your objection. You will have an opportunity on re-direct to in your mind clarify anything that the witness does not understand. He is a Professor of law with many years of experience. He has answered the question. You will have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Professor, let me ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: When the death penalty was in effect, typically the maximum would be 15 years or the death penalty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then the death penalty was obviously used for those persons who were considered to be the most serious violators and obviously beyond rehabilitation. They were a threat to society and it was determined, rightfully or wrongfully, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That (inaudible). The judge, though, under certain circumstances could still choose not to sentence the individual to the death penalty but instead give him or her 20 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that then recognition of the fact that there are individuals who must be punished, punished for their crimes as opposed to rehabilitated, but not go so far as to pronounce the death penalty on them? I think that's the essence of Mr. Niemann's question, and if you don't know, you may not know, and then we will go on to another area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is impossible not to know that, because there isn't a single criminal lawyer that has not studied the death penalty anywhere or at some time. Therefore, I am again risking that you will say that it is my personal opinion, but it is also the view of the legislator, I think, that the death penalty is collapsed, is a fiasco of all noble feelings and faith in man in any society, and that is why the legislator has limited this to a minimum. I must tell you that in the former Yugoslavia, SFRY, there were maybe one to two death penalties up to 1991 a year throughout Yugoslavia, which has now been reduced to a piece of that former Yugoslavia. Therefore, it is something so exceptional that I don't feel well if I were to say that the judge was being revengeful in his sentencing rather than doing what he had to. I think anyone who hears that a death penalty has been pronounced, he knows that this is a relic which was present in our case until recently unfortunately, but I find comfort in the fact that there are a number of codes in the world left that still retain the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the 20 year penalty? That was my question. I wasn't talking about the death penalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose, the purpose of the 20 years. The legislator tried to give a last chance to the offender to preserve him from total exclusion from society, from total destruction and removal from society. Let me give you an example. If somebody committed a terribly ruthless criminal offence and then one of the mitigating circumstances was found, those that I mentioned, then the court would sentence him to 20 years in the belief, in the conviction that 20 years is a very severe penalty, and it has a very detrimental effect on the psyche of the prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I want to move on to something else, if I may. Professor, is there or was there or has there ever been in the former Yugoslavia or any of the republics of the former Yugoslavia any system sponsored by the government or other organisation of state to assist the victims of crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To assist the victims of crime? Could you explain that for me, please? Which kind of criminals?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there any mechanism available where people who have been robbed, raped or badly assaulted or otherwise affected by criminals, where they can recover damages for the injuries that they have suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I have to say that in Belgrade in particular, as the capital of our country, we have telephone for raped women, a phone number for women suffering beatings and injuries in the home, and these kinds of services extend assistance to the victims to attain justice. They can accommodate them outside their homes in the case of assault in marriage. There are such things but the standard procedures are lawyers providing counsel and for the poor, the indigent, they are entitled to defence too, and then we have something else attached to all the municipalities. There are committees or some kind of legal assistance it is called, which is given by the municipality free of charge. If I was damaged, for instance, I can go to my municipality, to the office, and ask the employee to compile a complaint on my behalf. That is something that exists and it has just occurred to me. Of course, in psychology departments we also have sections dealing with the victims of war and providing assistance to people who need to be assisted in the removal of stress, which necessarily accompanies war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, you said that you had a seven person rule of someone affected by having to serve a sentence, and the effect that it has. You would agree with me that probably equally the same number of persons or probably more may well be affected if they were victims of crime. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, and those persons, the victims, or people close to the victims, suffer much more than these other seven that I mentioned. This is just an arbitrary number that I have chosen, but I think it corresponds to the truth more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me also that victims who have been very badly affected by crime may also find it hard to find their place in the sun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. That is why these services exist, those that I have referred to, to overcome stress, but I think it is up to every society to extend a helping hand to those victims, because they badly need that assistance and more quickly than the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour. I think that what the Professor was intending to say as a Professor, he said it, and the Prosecutor's question is not so much a matter of law as a matter of other sciences to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, please don't -- that's not appropriate really, to comment on questioning by counsel. We try to be very nice to each other in this courtroom at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Professor, as I understand it, the possibility of imposing a 20 year sentence only arose in the event of a death penalty being thought to be otherwise justifiable. It was a substitute for the death penalty. My question to you is: what happened after the abolition in parts of Yugoslavia at least of the death penalty? Was it still possible to impose a 20 year sentence or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The death penalty and the 20 year sentence, this 20 year sentence is called an alternative penalty in lieu of death. So when the death penalty is abolished, there will be no 20 year sentence, but the new law will probably provide for something like lifelong imprisonment or a substitute for that. I don't know. But there can't be an alternative penalty if there isn't the original penalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. That's the problem that I'm directing my question to, and without speculating on what the future law may be, life imprisonment or otherwise, the position at the moment, I suppose, is that since 20 years was only as an alternative to the death penalty, once the death penalty has gone, 20 years cannot be imposed; that's your understanding, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Certainly. It is an alternative penalty. It is imposed instead of. The judge cannot stand up and say: "I convict you to 20 years". He stands up and says: "I sentence you to death, but because of various mitigating circumstances I am changing that sentence to 20 year's imprisonment", now when the death penalty is completely abolished, the legislator will have to find some other solutions. Some way out has to be found. I do not wish to convey my opinion, because there's no need for that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, I do not ask you for that. Then we find that the abolition of the death penalty has been piecemeal. It occurred, as I understand it, in about 1990 in Slovenia. You say that only two or three years ago it occurred in Serbia. Does that mean that during that piecemeal process you had parts of Yugoslavia where the 20 years could be ordered and other parts where it could not be, or did it depend on whether the offence was a state offence or a Federal offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was probably not precise enough when I referred to Slovenia. There was the death penalty in Slovenia in the law but it was not pronounced for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am only concerned with the law, not what was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It existed. It existed until Yugoslavia broke up. It existed in all the laws of all the republics, but with the change and the formation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the constitution provides for the abolition of the death penalty, and now it's simply a question of the adjustment of the law. I don't know whether you are interested, but in practice it is very, very rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. Can you then give us a date when you say this change took place and the death penalty was abolished for the whole of Yugoslavia, because I had thought that it differed, depending on the particular republic. Can you give me a date when you say ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the SFRY, the former Yugoslavia, up to 1991, shall we say, the death penalty was provided for in all the laws of the republics and all others. Now it is another matter whether it was implemented. But when Yugoslavia broke up after the Badinter Commission and its opinion, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia passed a constitution. Was it 1992 or 1993? These younger colleagues of mine remember the dates better than me. The constitution was promulgated, which abolished the death penalty in the Federal constitution, but the problem was that Montenegro does not have the death penalty, and Serbia had it from before, and this still hasn't changed. I know it seems very illogical to you, but I'm quite frank here speaking before this Trial Chamber, and I'm telling you the situation as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you an entirely different question? The Federal Criminal Code, you, of course, are very familiar with. There's an Article in it, Article 142. I don't know if you are familiar with that Article, which deals with various crimes against civilian populations in a situation of war. That appears to mirror Geneva Convention 4. Is there any -- that you are aware of -- any similar Article in the Penal Code, the Federal Penal Code, dealing with the crimes against humanity, or dealing with common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions common to all those conventions? I don't know if you can help me on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Geneva Conventions, like other humanitarian conventions, that apply in particular to international crimes against humanity and the civilian population, are an obligation for Yugoslavia, as we were a signatory. Being an obligation, they have been incorporated in the criminal code, but those conventions, if I remember well, do not envisage necessarily the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not concerned with the death penalty at all. All I'm asking you is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we are under obligation. We signed that convention and it has been incorporated in the national legislation. That is the standard method of acceding to a convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If I can put my question perhaps more clearly: do you know whether that category of humanitarian -- international humanitarian law, commonly described as crimes against humanity, have made their appearances in any particular Article of the Federal Penal Code?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the chapter which is headed as you said. In the initial chapters there is mention made of the crimes against humanity. I don't know the exact titles, but there's a whole series of Articles regarding treatment of prisoners, of the wounded, civilian population, the children and all that. All that is absolutely listed in the Criminal Penal Code -- in the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Just one question, Professor. You indicated in 1992 or in 1993 the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia abolished by constitution at least the death penalty. In the materials submitted by the Prosecution they have made reference to other republics abolishing the death penalty. There's no indication, though, unless I'm wrong, about the status in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you know whether Bosnia and Herzegovina has by constitution at least abolished the death penalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say that I'm not familiar with the new legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I believe that they support the same trend as in Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That would be to abolish the death penalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's like a sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have additional questions of the Professor?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would ask for a brief pause if we could consult with our client, Mr. Tadic just for a minute, please. We would ask the indulgence of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We normally take a recess at 4, and so we will take a recess now. Does that relate to whether you have additional questions of the Professor?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. We will stand in recess until 4.20. (4.05 pm) (Short break) (4.20 pm) (Witness re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, we have only a few additional questions related to the system of criminal legislation in Yugoslavia. Is it possible in Yugoslavia for one accused person to stand on trial simultaneously for a few crimes vis-à-vis one person? To be clear, I'll take an example. If he was charged with murder, can he be pronounced guilty also of having inflicted suffering or heavy wounds on that same person who was murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The customary method is that the gravest crime consummates the previous. It would be very strange if somebody murders someone that he is also being tried for having beaten that person or broken his teeth or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So this overall punishment in that case consummates that. I am just interested in whether he can be proclaimed guilty for several crimes or only murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only one, murder, because murder consummates all the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So can it be said that the gravest crime he can be charged with consummates all the other crimes he can be charged with in such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think the list, the order is indisputable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So bodily injury is less important than life itself, and when a sentence is passed and when there are found -- when a verdict is pronounced of being guilty, does the court take into account the responsibility of all concerned and if, for example, the maximum sentence that can be pronounced is 15 years, and if a 13 year sentence is pronounced, do the others involved get lesser sentences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps. I wasn't clear before because everybody is held responsible within the framework of his or her intent, but the total of 15 years cannot be exceeded. That is the ceiling of punishment in Yugoslavia, whereas the other participants, especially if someone gave up voluntarily, the other accomplice can even be freed, whereas the main culprit can get 13 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is it possible for the first indicted person to be sentenced to 13 years and the other 7 years and the third one 3 years, etc.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is up to the court. Depending on the extent to which he deserves such punishment, what he did, the degree of culpability, attitude, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: So whether he was a subordinate or actively involved or only present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly all of that is taken into account. There are cases that we call in Yugoslavia in Latin "dolus resource" (sic). We can use somebody to do something without that person being aware of that crime. I as the instigator are going to be more responsible than the person who was used. Sorry, I should just add that the maximum of 15 years cannot be exceeded. That is the ceiling in Yugoslav legislation and the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Just one more thing, Professor. You said that these figures were outdated. I am interested in the practice in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia now when imposing criminal sanctions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I cannot give an exact explanation, but if you look at the annual reports for sanctions and crimes that is made by the statistical office of Yugoslavia, by the department for the judiciary within that office shows that the punishment for certain crimes is around the minimum, if I can use that expression, and the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: What is the minimum punishment envisaged for crimes against humanity? Is it true it is five years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From five years onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, additional cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: A couple of questions, Professor. In response to Mr. Vujin's question regarding sentencing for the gravest crime, so that if you sentenced a person for murder, if he also in the process of murdering, as you said, broke arms or something, obviously you would not sentence for that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite correct. He is sentenced for murder, but there are also qualified forms of murder, whether this is done in a particularly ruthless way and whether pain is inflicted upon the victim before death, but what happens in practice regrettably, for example, cutting up a corpse, that is not taken into account to such a large extent, because the victim does not suffer pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: And are you referring to when there is one victim, I gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'm talking about one victim, but ruthlessness towards several people, towards prisoners, is certainly an aggravating circumstance in our position to the mitigating circumstance that I spoke of, it is only natural in the Criminal Code that there are aggravating circumstances too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are there certain crimes -- let me put it this way -- are there certain acts that could be committed by an individual that may result in more than one crime because of the different elements that crimes have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question once again. Perhaps the translation wasn't good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I'm sure the translation was wonderful. In our statute without delving too deeply, for example, we may have a crime against humanity. We have may also have a crime that is denominated laws or customs of war. An individual commits an act and because of that act a factual determination is made that he has committed the act beyond reasonable doubt and then you look to determine whether or not that act constitutes a criminal offence. You then look at the elements for the offences and you may find that, for example, crimes against humanity may require certain elements and laws or customs of war require different elements. In your system would a person -- could a person be sentenced under crimes for -- for committing a crime against humanity as well as committing a law or custom of war, because the acts, although the same, involve different elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your question is not an easy one at all, because I must say that until 1991 we had such cases very rarely. Immediately after the Second World War when war criminals were tried, war criminals of the Wehrmacht, Germany, but then there was an interval during which there were not such cases. Sporadically there were cases that a war criminal would be discovered subsequently much later and he would be brought before a court of justice then, but now the situation is different. A distinction should not be made. After all a grave crime consumes a lesser crime. That would be a general rule. I'm sorry for not being in a position to give you a better answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vujin, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I would like to ask the parties, before we excuse the Professor, because perhaps he can be of assistance, I would like you, Mr. Vujin, and you, Mr. Niemann, to provide the Trial Chamber as quickly as possible with information regarding the status of the death penalty in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is if it was abolished, when it was abolished; if it was abolished by constitution, we would like a citation to the constitutional provision, and if a determination can be made of what is the practice of sentencing since the death penalty has been abolished, if it has been abolished, what that practice is and what evidence there is of that practice. Is there anything else? Okay. How quickly can that be provided do you believe? Monday? Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are optimistic we may be able to provide it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: An effort will be made to provide it tomorrow by the Prosecution. Please make sure the Defence has a copy of whatever is provided. Then, Mr. Vujin, we would like the position of the Defence as to the material provided by the Prosecutor. Thank you, Professor. You are excused. Thank you very much for coming to us and talking to us about these issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just have one question, your Honour. The administration of your Tribunal informed me two days ago that I wouldn't be needed by the court and that I could go back tomorrow, because I came here not to address the administration but the Chamber. I would like to hear it from the Chamber whether I can travel back to my country tomorrow. I don't like it when the administration decides about me and prepares my return ticket, etc. I hope that you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do understand you. I share your views. As far as I'm concerned, and I hope I have sufficient authority, you are excused and you may leave tomorrow. The parties have no objection. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I can leave tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. It was a great honour: (Witness withdraws from court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vujin, I understand that you do not have additional witnesses at this time except for Dr. Nedopil, who will be here on Friday, and we will hear from him after we complete the initial appearance on Friday, which begins at 10. So in the vicinity of 11 o'clock we will begin to hear from him. Now we wanted to hear the positions from counsel as to the appropriate sentence. The Prosecution is to proceed first. Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the psychiatric reports that we have given to the Defence, and there is agreement that they can be handed up to the court. The translation is satisfactory for their purposes. I tender them now. Because they come from us they may be Prosecution Exhibit 373. In handing them up, your Honour, I note that there is reference in them to witnesses, at least one witness who is given protection, so it may be appropriate, your Honour, if rather than breach your Honours' orders in relation to the witness protection that they be marked confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They can either be marked confidential or the references can be redacted, however you wish to handle it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just confidential would satisfy our requirements, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any objection, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.
