utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine. Then Prosecution Exhibit 373 will be admitted and it will be admitted as confidential under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me just a minute. (Pause) Yes, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I notice the time is twenty to five. I could well finish by 5.30 but if I am not finished by then, I would not expect to be more than ten minutes beyond that. If your Honours would indulge me, I would prefer to complete my address today if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We would indulgence even if it is more than ten minutes but not more than 15. Take your time and use what time is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this situation I do not wish to cover anything that we have referred to in our brief, unless your Honours have questions on any of the matters we raised in the brief. Your Honour, under Article 24, paragraph 2 and Rule 101 of the Rules there is provided that in determining the sentence the Trial Chamber shall take into account, and I mention the relevant matters for these proceedings: the gravity of the offence, the individual circumstances of the accused, mitigating circumstances including co-operation with the Prosecutor and the sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia. The Trial Chamber is also required to indicate whether multiple sentences are to be served concurrently or consecutively and credits to be given for time spent in custody prior to surrender and prior to trial. I shall now deal with each one of these issues one by one. Turning, firstly, to the gravity of the offence, the convicted person, Tadic, has been found guilty of five counts of war crimes and six counts of crimes against humanity. A crime against humanity is of the same species as genocide and after genocide is the most heinous crime in the jurisdiction of the Tribunal and, of course, one of the most serious crimes that anyone can be convicted of. Under the Nuremberg Charter the penalty for a person convicted of a crime against humanity was either the death penalty or any other penalty deemed just. States which included crimes against humanity in their national criminal laws have almost universally prescribed the most severe penalty permitted in their system for the commission of this offence. In the sentencing decision of the Trial Chamber in Erdemovic at paragraph 28, page 14, the Chamber, when speaking of the seriousness of crimes against humanity, said: "Crimes against humanity are serious acts of violence which harm human beings by striking what is most essential to them: their life, liberty, physical welfare, health or dignity. They are inhumane acts that by their extent and gravity go beyond the limits tolerable to the international community, which must per force demand their punishment. But crimes against humanity also transcend the individual, because when the individual is assaulted, humanity comes under attack and is negated. It is therefore the concept of humanity as victim which essentially characterises crimes against humanity". Professor Bassiouni, when describing the nature of crimes against humanity, said in relation to the Nuremberg Charter: "The Charter establishes a generic criminal category labelled "crimes against humanity" to fit the unforeseen and unforeseeable depredations and only the unbridled nefarious imagination of evil and banal men could have actuated. Indeed, the facts that gave rise to "crimes against humanity" were too barbarous to foresee and thus no specific positive law existed that covered all the misdeeds committed". This is a quote from Professor Bassiouni's book entitled "Crimes Against Humanity in International Law: The Netherlands", Martinus Nijhoff Publishers, (1992), page 149. Count 1, the persecution count, is in our submission a particularly serious crime. It was an evil crime. The convicted person, Tadic, had no reason to do what he did. He did it out of greed, hatred, jealousy and intolerance. Politically motivated, he joined the push for greater Serbia and the Muslim population were in the road. Tadic was two-faced. He portrayed himself as a friend of the Muslims but obviously at all times harbouring a deep hatred of these people who had extended to him the hand of friendship. Clearly he resented deeply being in the minority in the town of Kozarac and waited for the day to arrive when the tables would turn. When the time came with enthusiasm he joined the forces of the Bosnia Serbs and assisted them in the task of ridding the area of the Muslims and Croats. As set out in our tendered declarations marked Prosecution Exhibit P371 and P372, the suffering that he personally was instrumental in causing to these people, his victims, is hard to fully comprehend, but he has been indirectly responsible for contributing to the devastation of the lives of the people in the Prijedor area, and for what egregious crimes were these tragic victims being so cruelly punished? Their crime is they were different. That's all. They were different. A crime against humanity is one of extreme gravity, demanding the most severe penalty. It is the most serious crime on the criminal calendar, and one should, in our submission, approach sentencing as one would ordinarily deal with the most serious crime in the criminal calendar. In some jurisdictions you have mandatory life sentences; in other jurisdictions you have the death penalty. In circumstances where you have multiple murders, then the court can impose multiple life sentences, or order that convicted persons serve the rest of their life in prison, or that the papers be marked "never to be paroled". In most jurisdictions life sentences are substantially reduced by remissions or parole. Thus, a life sentence can mean less than 15 years served, unless the court otherwise orders. It is the position of the Prosecutor that with respect to crimes against humanity one starts with a sentence of life imprisonment. One must consider the possibility of multiple life sentences for multiple convictions of crimes against humanity. Depending on whether the sentence is remitted or paroled, one must consider whether or not the sentences should be served consecutively or concurrently, or expressed differently, whether all the sentences should start and end on the same date. For separate events involving crimes of similar gravity, where the crimes are very serious, there is no reason in our submission consistent with logic why the sentences should be concurrent. The overall offending in this case is not the most serious likely to come before this Tribunal, but it is certainly not to be regarded as minor offending either. The personal culpability however and the evil he perpetrated is one of the most sinister and serious in nature. However, we are not pressing for multiple life sentences, nor are we suggesting that sentences should be served consecutively. It is our submission that with respect to Count 1, your Honours' consideration should commence with a sentence of life imprisonment. In respect to the other crimes against humanity, your Honours might consider imposing a very severe sentence of less than life imprisonment, but for such sentences to be served concurrent with the sentence of life imprisonment. In our submission the war crimes counts should attract a lesser penalty than the crimes against humanity, and these, too, should be concurrent with the other sentences. In relation to all the offences, your Honours may wish to consider making a recommendation that all the sentences should earn remission at the same rate as other prisoners serving similar sentences in the institution where the accused is to serve his sentence should apply. I now turn, your Honours, to the individual circumstances of the accused. At the time of the commission of the crimes charged in the indictment the convicted person Tadic was 36 and a half years of age. He was married with two children. He had lived in Kozarac for the most part of his life and he knew most of its inhabitants. In our submission it is not possible for Tadic to paint a picture of himself as a young, inexperienced man, tragically caught up in the horrors of war, from which he could not escape or fail to participate. There is absolutely no evidence to suggest that Tadic had to commit any of the crimes for which he has been found guilty. On his evidence he was a traffic policeman. His wife and family were given privileged status. He did not have to go to the camps at Omarska, Trnopolje or Keraterm and when there, to cruelly beat, torture and depravely molest the prisoners. He did not have to actively and enthusiastically participate in the rounding up, torture and murder of the unfortunate non-Serb victims in Kozarac and then to take from these helpless souls their lives, possessions, their children and their relatives. Nor was Tadic motivated to do what he did because he was compelled to carry out the wishes of the state under threat of punishment. No. He enthusiastically participated in this evil plan of the state as a willing worker, one of Karadzic's henchmen, and in his depravity he sought recognition. He expected to be endowed with gifts and favours by corrupt but grateful officials of an evil administration. There is nothing sinister in Tadic's family background to engender any sympathy. He does not come from a tragic family background. He was not deprived or abused in his youth. He does not appear to have suffered any great personal tragedy in his life, which would cause him to unwittingly stumble into this situation. He came from a solid family background. His father was a respected Second World War hero. Compared to his fellow citizens in Kozarac, he was not underprivileged or discriminated against in any way. He was respected and liked in the community. What then could possibly have motivated him to commit the outrageous crimes for which he has been found guilty? The answer, in our submission, is clear. It was greed and power. If the Muslims and Croats were out of the area, then this meant more for the Bosnia Serbs, and if this meant more for the Bosnia Serbs, then it meant more for Tadic. Accordingly, there is nothing in the individual circumstances or background of Tadic which in our submission would justify a reduction of the sentence the court would otherwise impose. Mitigating circumstances, including co-operation with the Prosecutor. The convicted person, Tadic, has done nothing to co-operate with the Prosecutor. He has shown absolutely no remorse for the crimes that he has committed, nor has he indicated in the slightest way that he is in any way sorry for the terrible tragedy that he has brought upon his hapless victims. This utter lack of remorse or appreciation of the nature of his crimes has continued over the period of the last few days. It is extraordinary that Tadic would continue to portray himself as a victim. This is the individual who was President of the Kozarac SDS, who was given the responsibility for conducting the plebiscite in Kozarac. He actively participated in the attack of Kozarac and the murder and torture of Muslims and Croats from the area. After that he was given what has been referred to as the privileged and safe position of a traffic policeman. He was appointed to the high position in Kozarac with control over the distribution of property and finally appointed as a Serbian Red Cross official, so that he had direct access to all the humanitarian aid coming into Kozarac. Then he claims that he has been persecuted by Prijedor officials. We believe the evidence suggests that was the result of a dispute between greedy officials, nothing that should engender sympathy from this Tribunal. Your Honours, it is instructive to compare the Erdemovic case with this case. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, has given extensive assistance to the Prosecutor. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, was prepared to surrender before he was indicted. In fact, unlike Tadic, there was no investigation going on in relation to him at the time he was prepared to surrender. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, made a full and free confession, without which no prosecution against him would have been commenced at that time. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, later voluntarily repeated his confession to the Trial Chamber. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, specifically sought his transfer to The Hague for trial. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, gave the Prosecutor extremely important information and leads which at the time was otherwise unobtainable. The information Erdemovic gave greatly assisted the Prosecution with on-going investigations. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, freely gave evidence in a Rule 61 hearing against Karadzic and Mladic. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, was a very young man of 23 years of age when he committed the crime. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, was the Bosnia Croat in a Bosnia Serb army. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, was in no way politically motivated to commit the crimes that he did. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, did not plan to commit the crime. He knew nothing about it until he was on the scene of the crime. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, did not commit the crime out of hatred or greed. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, simply obeyed orders under threat of death or punishment. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, clearly demonstrated that he was disgusted and appalled at the fact that he had participated in such a terrible crime. Erdemovic, unlike Tadic, was convicted and sentenced on only one count of a crime against humanity. Erdemovic was sentenced to ten year's imprisonment. In our submission co-operation with the Prosecutor should be substantially rewarded by giving a significant reduction in the sentence, 50-75 per cent off the sentence than would otherwise be imposed, had it not been for the co-operation, is in some circumstances justified in our view. The Prosecutor of the Tribunal is confronted with a great many more obstacles than that normally encountered by police in domestic settings. The Prosecutor has limited access to the scene of the crime and to many of the potential witnesses. Indeed, in the place where both Erdemovic and Tadic committed their crimes, there was outright hostility at the time towards investigators from the Tribunal. Even unobstructed access to the crime scene involves very expensive and difficult travel from The Hague to the Balkans. Accordingly in the investigations undertaken by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal there are often many missing pieces to the jigsaw that the Prosecutor has enormous difficulty in filling. One co-operative participant such as Erdemovic can save the international community huge sums of money which would otherwise have to be spent on lengthy and detailed investigative work. Very important information can mean the difference between a prosecution or not. Further, the Prosecution has much difficulty in getting the accused persons arrested and brought before the Tribunal for trial. Strong consideration should be given to those who voluntarily surrender. The Prosecution sees great value in sending a clear signal to non asserted persons that people who co-operate with the Tribunal in terms of providing information, who voluntarily confess to their crimes, plead guilty, voluntarily surrender, will get favourable considerations for those acts and may receive a significant reduction in the sentence they would otherwise receive. More importantly, such co-operation also says a great deal about the true character of an individual and the remorse, if any, he feels for the crimes that he has committed. The Prosecutor takes the view that people such as Tadic, who have not done any of these things, cannot expect any or any significant mitigation of the sentence. In our submission, the convicted person, Tadic, should get no mitigation of his sentence under this heading. I turn now, your Honours, to the sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia. In the former Yugoslavia serious crimes of this nature could in 1992 attract the death penalty. Subsequently the death penalty has been abolished. Prior to the abolition of the death penalty the prevailing attitude to sentencing was that life imprisonment was considered too cruel a treatment. Presumably the death penalty was not so considered. In any case a serious offender received the death penalty or 15 year's imprisonment. Following the abolition of the death penalty, judges were given the option of sentencing an offender to a term of imprisonment of up to 20 years, but this was considered to be an exception. Accordingly, when the Tribunal created its Rules of Procedure and Evidence, there was no power for a court in the former Yugoslavia to impose a life sentence on an offender, no matter how serious the offending. This matter was specifically addressed by the court, by the Chamber in the Erdemovic case. In Erdemovic in the sentencing decision, page 33 -- paragraph 33, the Trial Chamber reviewed the meaning of the reference to "recourse to the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia" as provided for in Article 24(1) and Rule 101 (A). The Chamber noted that at the time of the commission of the crimes the republics had no equivalent provisions to crimes against humanity. However, articles 141-156 of Chapter 14 of the Federal Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia covered inter alia genocide and war crimes perpetrated against the civilian population. The Chamber in Erdemovic then noted that the minimum terms of imprisonment that could be imposed for crimes was five years with a maximum of 15 years with a provision of a term of 20 years that could be imposed if substitution of the death penalty or for aggravated instances of the offence. The Trial Chamber then noted that there was no direct equivalent of the Tribunal's Article 5 in the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, and then concluded that the only principle that should be given weight when examining the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia is that for offences of this kind the most severe penalty available should be applied. That's at paragraph 35, if your Honours please. The Trial Chamber then observed there was no court decision from the former Yugoslavia available for crimes of this nature that could usefully assist the Tribunal in drawing conclusions as to their sentencing practices. The argument that the reference to the general practice regarding prison sentences in the former Yugoslavia was to overcome any objections arising due to the principle of "nullum crimen" was rejected by the Chamber on the basis that such an argument defeats the universal nature of these crimes. Your Honours said that at paragraph 38. The trial chamber then said that the reference to the general practice in Yugoslavia was for guidance purposes only and was not to be considered binding. It said: "Whenever possible, the international Tribunal will review the relevant legal practices of the former Yugoslavia, but will not be bound in any way by those practices in the penalties it establishes and the sentence it is imposes for the crimes falling within its jurisdiction". That's at paragraph 40, if your Honours please. They then go on to say with respect to the overall aims of punishment, different national jurisdictions have different objectives in mind when determining what the appropriate punishment for a crime should be. In a national context, the state has a particular interest in trying to achieve the rehabilitation of its citizens who have fallen foul of the law. I am going on to my submission as opposed to what your Honours say. This is so because there is a particular need to facilitate the smooth running of society. Accordingly, when the paramount interest, having regard to a particular criminal and his crimes, is the protection of society, the death penalty might be imposed, should it be available. If protection of society is not of such importance, then rehabilitation of the individual may play a more important role. In the former Yugoslavia, the principle of sentencing that seems to have prevailed was that if the only consideration was to protect society from the criminal, then the death sentence when the death sentence was available was the appropriate sentencing disposition, but if this was not the case, then life imprisonment was not considered conducive to rehabilitation, so the 15 year maximum sentence was devised. Any sentence for longer than 15 years was considered to be inhumane. However, after the abolition of the death penalty, provision was made for a 20 year sentence. As we have heard in evidence today, your Honours, the position seems to be in a statement of flux, moving from the period when the death penalty was in operation to something else, but we don't know what that is. One must also consider that the sentencing practices, the penal systems and conditions of confinement are developed and implemented pursuant to that particular society's norms and values, and one cannot automatically, in our submission, transpose those to the International Tribunal, whose obligation is to enforce the values, norms and expectations of the wider international community. When it comes to devising an appropriate sentence and policy for this Tribunal, in our submission rehabilitation would seem to be the least appropriate aim of any sentencing policy. The Tribunal cannot adequately supervise or devise suitable rehabilitative programmes for persons that it imprisons, nor is it reasonable if such programmes were devised to impose any such programmes on a state good enough to offer its prison facilities for the purposes of imprisoning convicted persons. That is not to say that convicted persons by this Tribunal will not ultimately be rehabilitated. Clearly we all hope that this will be so, but our submission is it clearly should form no part or no significant part of the sentencing regime the Tribunal adopts. While there are no doubt other sentencing objectives that may appropriately play a role, clearly in our submission the dominant centre piece of any sentencing policy devised by this Tribunal should be the principle that criminologists refer to as the principle of "just desserts", punishment. It seems to us that if one of the primary functions of this Tribunal is to contribute to a restoration of true peace in the former Yugoslavia, and the re-establishment of their fractured society, then this will not be achieved, in our submission, if the Tribunal concerns itself with the speculative concept of the rehabilitative needs of the individual perpetrators and pays insufficient regard to the need to ensure that those responsible for these heinous crimes are brought to justice and dealt with according to law. In our respectful submission, the most effective way in which this can be assured in relation to the convicted person Tadic is to impose upon him a life sentence of imprisonment. They are our submissions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I have two questions. The first one stems really from your suggestion that life imprisonment was appropriate in relation to paragraph 1, persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You then went on to say that there should be remissions granted similarly to those remissions that are granted to other prisoners in the particular jail system in which the accused found himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How do you work that out? Remission may be of one-third of the sentence or so many years. How does that accord with a life sentence? Obviously you can't have a proportion of it remitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, in some jurisdictions now, as your Honour is probably aware, there is the traditional life sentence, where someone serves it for life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It means much less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It means nothing like that any more. It means you serve a period of time and after a period of time you are entitled to a remission. Generally speaking -- I mean, we have not done a complete survey, but in a number of jurisdictions it can mean something like 15 years and less, but if, for example, a person is convicted -- sentenced to 15 years and at the same time earns remissions, well, that might mean ten years or nine years or something like that, if remissions apply. The only submission that we can make in this, because we have no idea where the accused person will be sent, is that if he is in an institution where the prisoners beside him are earning remissions of their sentence for their life sentence or whatever is equivalent in that jurisdiction, then our submission is that in this case, and we are not suggesting that it's something that should universally apply, but in this case we say that this particular convicted person should enjoy the benefit of remissions that his co-fellow prisoners would be earning, other than him go there and to be alongside prisoners convicted of life imprisonment and for him not to earn remissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, although the imprisonment for life, you suggest that we should impose what it means, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am not asking your Honour to do that in the sense that we are saying if remissions are available to this accused per force of the fact that he goes to an institution where remissions are earned, and in most institutions that is certainly becoming the norm, then we are saying that the Chamber may care to recommend that he should earn remissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. My point, I think, is this: he may well be in a system which regards life as meaning 12 years or 15 years, whereas the sentence that you are suggesting we should impose would mean for the term of his natural life. The two are not comparable. I don't see how you can work in a remission system applicable to life meaning 12 or 15 years to a term of natural life sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me just add a little bit to that, maybe perhaps a little complexity. The Tribunal presently has agreements only with two countries, Italy and Finland, I believe, that will accept persons that are convicted by the Tribunal and the agreement, of course, speaks for itself, but there are certain limitations that the Tribunal has attempted to impose, but there are certain limitations that we cannot impose. So we need to keep that in mind in terms of any recommendation that we may make, because the agreement itself I would imagine would have to be complied with, and if any recommendation that we make would be contrary to that, there would be a problem. With respect to remissions, though, if, for example -- you use the term "remission". In my system we don't usually use the word "remission". We think of that as something the court might do unilaterally and that is remit or lower the sentence. You are simply requesting we would sentence to life imprisonment, and then the accused would then serve in this instance either in Finland or Italy, unless I'm not aware of another agreement, and then if that state has a system of remitting or reducing life imprisonment to 15 years, assuming good behaviour, then you are suggesting that the same rule apply to Mr. Tadic. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, in that institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: All we would do would be sentence and then the rules applicable in that institution would also apply to Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The term remission is a little problematic to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be a problematic term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I still don't follow you. Take the case of Finland. Assume life means 15 years. The sort of remission I thought you were talking about was that person so sentenced would probably not serve 15 years because there would be remissions and they might only serve seven years. Is it the reduction of our term of natural life to 15 years you are talking about, or the benefit of the further reduction that is granted to those who have got a Finnish sentence of life, which means 15, but, in fact, they get out after seven. They are two differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand. In some jurisdictions your Honour, what happens is the person is sentenced to life imprisonment and then the court orders there be a non-parole period, that the person serve a certain number of years and there be no parole during that period. That reduces it to an actual figure so that the convicted person knows that after this period they will get paroled. In addition to that -- in other jurisdictions the court doesn't make such an order. It simply imposes a period of life imprisonment and then the local administrative prison authorities or justice department or whatever then itself determines parole. It interviews the prisoner and grants parole after a certain period. That can also apply to life sentences unless, of course, the court has made an order that he is never to be paroled or released, whichever way the court expresses itself. Now in addition to that prisoners can have the sentence reduced by prison authorities by remissions for good behaviour, so that when a person is in prison there is an incentive, as it were, for the prisoner to behave and to rehabilitate. Now what we are saying is that we understand there's no provision for your Honours to impose a non-parole period, but if there is a regime in place at that institution which would permit a reduction of the sentence either by a combination of parole or just straight out remissions, then we submit in this case, and we are selective in this, that the accused person, Tadic, should have the benefit of that, and we say it for two reasons: one, because it is not the most serious offending that is going to come before this Tribunal, and we submit that this would be some recognition of that, not moving away from the fact that we submit that a sentence of life imprisonment is the only appropriate sentencing disposition, but this would give some measure of reduction of that, and in addition to that, it is better for the convicted person in an institution side by side with other prisoners who have committed offences in that society to be on an equal footing, to allow that person to have the sentence reduced according to the regime that applies there. We submit in relation to this convicted person, that is a measure that is appropriate, having regard to his offending. Now whether it is achievable or whether the state that takes the person is prepared to do that is another question but it seems in our submission not inappropriate to make a recommendation, if your Honours are so disposed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That was my first question. I had a second one. I noticed that in questioning the last witness and again in your oral submissions you said that the -- it was after the abolition of the death penalty in the former Yugoslavia that the 20 year term was conceived as an alternative. My understanding, I must say, was that the alternative 20 years long preceded the abolition of the death penalty and went hand in hand with it at the time when it existed. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I confess, your Honour, I am no expert in their law but my understanding of the law was the 20 years was introduced as a late measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: After the abolition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might just ... would your Honours excuse me a moment? (Pause.) I may well have misspoke, your Honours, and for that I apologise. It appears there was a period of time when both the 20 year period and the death penalty were standing side by side. What I cannot assist your Honours with at the moment but I will endeavour to do so is when that came in and for what period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Those dates would be very useful to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Unless there are any other matters, your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, would you like to begin your submissions, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, considering the time -- I'm sorry. Considering that it is ten minutes to the time envisaged for adjournment and in view of the fact that the Defence could use some consultations, we would beg to have the opportunity to begin our statement tomorrow. We believe there will be enough time for us to complete it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Every day we have been together, Mr. Vujin, you have asked for us to adjourn early. If we were in a trial that lasted seven months, I suppose if you added up all of that time, it might last for several weeks that we would lose but we are not in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: It was not so much on our account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We are not in that situation and we are trying to be flexible. So we will adjourn and resume tomorrow at 2.30 with the Defence submissions. (5.20 pm)

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until tomorrow afternoon at 2.30 pm)
